subject: biology
topicDisplay: B3–B4 — Form and function: organisms and ecosystems
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
Blocked coronary arteries, and what correlations can prove
Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
Finding a limit with a transect
Temperature and rainfall set the biome
Niche is a role, not a place
Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse

questions.q: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?
options: The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.
optionWhy: Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large organism has proportionally less surface across which to exchange gases, and its inner cells are too far from the surface for diffusion alone to supply them. Both effects make specialized gas-exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

A student who reasons that a bigger organism has 'more surface' picks this. Total surface area does increase, but the ratio of surface to volume decreases, so there is less surface per unit of respiring tissue, not more.

A student who equates gas exchange with breathing picks this. Gas exchange is a vital function in all organisms, including unicellular organisms and plants; the challenge grows with size because the surface area-to-volume ratio falls and the diffusion distance rises, not because small organisms do not exchange gases.

A student who thinks diffusion is fast over any distance picks this. Diffusion time rises steeply with distance, and the distance from centre to exterior grows with size, so distance is one of the two reasons the challenge increases.
questions.explain: Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large organism has proportionally less surface across which to exchange gases, and its inner cells are too far from the surface for diffusion alone to supply them. Both effects make specialized gas-exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

questions.q: A fish rests in still, well-oxygenated water. What keeps the oxygen concentration gradient across its gill surface steep?
options: The water around the gills contains dissolved oxygen, so the gradient is maintained by the water itself.
Once oxygen has diffused into the blood the gradient is fixed and does not need to be maintained further.
Blood is held in the gill capillaries until it is saturated, so that every red blood cell loads fully.
Water is pumped over the gills while blood flows continuously through their dense capillaries.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gills need no ventilation picks this. The layer of water in contact with the gill surface is depleted of oxygen within moments, and diffusion through still water is very slow, so the fish must pump fresh water over the gills.
A student who believes a gradient looks after itself picks this. Diffusion destroys the gradient that drives it, so it must be continuously renewed by ventilation and blood flow.

A student who thinks blood loads more if it lingers picks this. Blood that stays approaches equilibrium with the water and net diffusion stops; continuous flow replaces it with deoxygenated blood, keeping the gradient steep.

Ventilation with water keeps the outer side of the gill surface rich in oxygen, and continuous blood flow through the dense network of capillaries keeps the inner side low in oxygen by carrying oxygenated blood away. Together they maintain the concentration gradient.
questions.explain: Ventilation with water keeps the outer side of the gill surface rich in oxygen, and continuous blood flow through the dense network of capillaries keeps the inner side low in oxygen by carrying oxygenated blood away. Together they maintain the concentration gradient.

questions.q: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?
options: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
optionWhy: A student who reverses cause and effect, as in the balloon model, picks this. The ribs and diaphragm move first, lowering the pressure in the lungs; air flows in because of that pressure difference.

A student who thinks the lungs are muscular picks this. Lungs contain no skeletal muscle; the thorax is enlarged by the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, and the lungs expand passively with it.

A student who pictures the diaphragm's dome as its active state picks this. A relaxed, domed diaphragm reduces thorax volume and belongs to expiration; in inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens.

Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax. The pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.
questions.explain: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax. The pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines vital capacity?
options: The maximum volume that can be inhaled in one breath from the end of a normal exhalation.
The maximum volume that can be exhaled after a normal, resting inhalation.
The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.
The total volume of air in the lungs when they are inflated as fully as possible.
optionWhy: A student who pictures 'capacity' as filling up from the resting position picks this. This is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve; vital capacity also includes the expiratory reserve that can be forced out below a normal breath.

A student who focuses on the exhalation into the spirometer and forgets the maximal inhalation first picks this. This is tidal volume plus expiratory reserve, which leaves out the inspiratory reserve.

Vital capacity runs from the peak of a maximal inhalation to the end of a maximal exhalation, and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve. It is measured by inhaling fully and then exhaling fully into a spirometer.

A student who reads 'capacity' as the whole contents of the lungs picks this. The lungs cannot be emptied completely by exhaling, so the total lung volume is larger than the vital capacity that a spirometer can measure.
questions.explain: Vital capacity runs from the peak of a maximal inhalation to the end of a maximal exhalation, and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve. It is measured by inhaling fully and then exhaling fully into a spirometer.

questions.q: Which statement about a plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf is correct?
options: It shows a few representative cells of each tissue in outline, including their nuclei and chloroplasts.
It shows the outline and position of each tissue, with the palisade mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis.
It shows each vein with phloem above the xylem, because the phloem lies nearer to the upper surface.
It shows the spongy mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis, above the palisade mesophyll.
optionWhy: A student who assumes every microscope drawing shows cells picks this. Individual cells belong in a high-power drawing; a plan diagram shows each tissue as a labelled region bounded by lines.

A plan diagram is a low-power drawing of tissue regions, not cells. From the upper surface down it shows upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis, with veins in the mesophyll; the palisade layer lies immediately under the upper epidermis where light enters.
A student who transfers the stem arrangement, phloem outside xylem, picks this. In a leaf vein the xylem lies toward the upper surface and the phloem toward the lower surface.
A student who has learnt the layers as a list without their positions picks this. The palisade mesophyll lies under the upper epidermis and the spongy mesophyll below it, above the lower epidermis.
questions.explain: A plan diagram is a low-power drawing of tissue regions, not cells. From the upper surface down it shows upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis, with veins in the mesophyll; the palisade layer lies immediately under the upper epidermis where light enters.

questions.q: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
options: It keeps the distance over which substances diffuse between blood and tissue cells very short.
It lets blood pass through the capillary faster, so that more blood reaches the tissue cells.
It leaves room for a lumen wide enough for red blood cells to pass through side by side.
It allows red blood cells to squeeze out through the wall and into the tissues.
optionWhy: Exchange across the capillary wall is by diffusion, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply as distance increases. A wall of a single endothelial cell keeps that distance to a minimum, so exchange is rapid.

A student who thinks a thin wall is an easy-flow pipe picks this. In fact blood flows more slowly in capillaries than in any other vessel; the thin wall shortens the diffusion distance, it does not speed the flow.

A student who believes a wider vessel is better for exchange picks this. In fact capillaries are narrow, with red blood cells passing in single file, which is what brings every cell close to the wall.

A student who pictures capillaries as full of large holes picks this. Red blood cells stay inside the capillary; the thin wall is about diffusion distance, and the fenestrations found in some capillaries are pores far too small for cells.
questions.explain: Exchange across the capillary wall is by diffusion, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply as distance increases. A wall of a single endothelial cell keeps that distance to a minimum, so exchange is rapid.

questions.q: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?
options: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the artery wall pumps like the gut wall picks this. Elastic tissue is not muscle and generates no propulsive wave; the heart provides the force that moves blood.

A student who equates a strong wall with a rigid wall picks this. A rigid artery would let pressure fall to zero between beats; elastic tissue is there precisely because the wall must stretch and recoil.

A student who gives valves an active pushing role picks this. Elastic tissue is not valve tissue and no valve, venous or cardiac, generates force; the artery's elastic tissue stretches and recoils to maintain pressure (B3.2.3).

The layers of muscle and elastic tissue allow the artery to withstand and maintain high pressure. Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy that the recoil returns during relaxation, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.
questions.explain: The layers of muscle and elastic tissue allow the artery to withstand and maintain high pressure. Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy that the recoil returns during relaxation, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

questions.q: Why can heart rate be determined by feeling the carotid or radial pulse with the fingertips?
options: Because blood is pushed past the fingertips in one surge each time the muscular artery wall contracts.
Because the blood flowing through the artery can be felt as it moves past the fingertips.
Because a pressure wave passes along the artery wall each time the left ventricle contracts.
Because these are the places where large veins close to the surface of the skin carry the heartbeat.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the artery wall pumps picks this. The artery does not contract to push each surge; it is stretched by the pressure wave from the ventricle.
A student who thinks the pulse is the movement of blood picks this. Blood flows continuously; what is felt is the intermittent pressure wave that stretches the wall.

Each ventricular contraction forces blood into the aorta and sends a pressure wave along the arteries. Where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the carotid or radial artery, the fingertips feel the wall expanding once per heartbeat, so counting pulses gives the heart rate.
A student who thinks the pulse is found in veins picks this. The carotid and radial pulses are arterial; the pressure wave has been lost by the time blood reaches the veins.
questions.explain: Each ventricular contraction forces blood into the aorta and sends a pressure wave along the arteries. Where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the carotid or radial artery, the fingertips feel the wall expanding once per heartbeat, so counting pulses gives the heart rate.

questions.q: A blood clot completely occludes a branch of a coronary artery. What is the direct consequence?
options: Blood can no longer pass through the chambers of the heart, so the heart stops beating almost at once.
The region of cardiac muscle supplied by that branch is deprived of oxygen and its cells die.
Fat from the diet keeps building up on the surface of the clot until the artery bursts open.
The muscle in the artery wall contracts to force the clot along, tearing the artery wall.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the coronary arteries are the route blood takes through the heart picks this. Blood continues to flow through the chambers; it is the muscle of the wall that loses its supply.

The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.
A student who holds the grease-in-a-drainpipe model picks this. Atheroma forms within the artery wall, and the consequence of occlusion is oxygen starvation of muscle, not bursting.
A student who thinks artery walls pump picks this. Artery muscle does not push contents along; the harm done by occlusion is to the cardiac muscle downstream.
questions.explain: The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.

questions.q: A student is drawing a plan diagram from a micrograph of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem. Which description matches what should be drawn?
options: A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the epidermis, and cortex outside the ring.
A single central mass of vascular tissue, with xylem forming a star and phloem between its arms, surrounded by a wide cortex.
A ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with phloem towards the centre and xylem towards the epidermis, and pith in the middle.
A wide cortex carrying water and sugars up the stem, with a thin ring of xylem and phloem that provides support only.
optionWhy: In a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring. Within each bundle the xylem lies on the inner side and the phloem on the outer side; the cortex lies between the ring and the single-layered epidermis, and pith fills the centre.
A student who expects transport tissue to run down the middle picks this. A central star of xylem is the arrangement in a root; a stem has a ring of separate vascular bundles.
A student who has reversed the two tissues within the bundle picks this. Xylem is on the inner side of each bundle, towards the centre; phloem is on the outer side.
A student who thinks the cortex is a transport tissue picks this. The cortex is storage and packing tissue; xylem and phloem in the vascular bundles carry out transport.
questions.explain: In a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring. Within each bundle the xylem lies on the inner side and the phloem on the outer side; the cortex lies between the ring and the single-layered epidermis, and pith fills the centre.

questions.q: Which statement gives the meaning of the term habitat as it is used in ecology?
options: The place in which a community, species, population or single organism lives.
The role that a species plays in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on.
A large region of the Earth that shares one type of climate, such as tundra.
The set of organisms of different species that live together in one area.
optionWhy: This is the definition used in the guide. A habitat is a place, and it can be the place where a whole community lives or where one organism lives; it is described by geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.
A student who merges an organism's way of life with where it lives picks this. The role a species plays is a different idea from its habitat, which is the place in which it lives.

A student who has met 'the tundra habitat' in general reading picks this. A region of shared climate is a biome; a habitat is the place where a particular organism, population or community lives and can be very small.

A student who attaches the word to the organisms rather than the place picks this. The organisms of different species living together are the community; the habitat is the place in which that community lives.
questions.explain: This is the definition used in the guide. A habitat is a place, and it can be the place where a whole community lives or where one organism lives; it is described by geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.

questions.q: Students are required to collect transect data from a natural or semi-natural habitat. Which of these sites is semi-natural?
options: A hay meadow that is cut once each year but is dominated by wild grasses and wildflowers.
A field of wheat grown from sown seed, with wild poppies growing along its margins.
A garden lawn sown with a bought seed mixture and mown every week through the summer.
A peat bog in a remote upland with no history of drainage, grazing or other management.
optionWhy: A semi-natural habitat has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Annual cutting is human influence; the wild grasses and flowers that dominate make the meadow semi-natural.
A student who takes the presence of any wild species as the test picks this. The field is dominated by a cultivated crop; a few wild poppies at the edge do not make it semi-natural.
A student who counts any green outdoor site as semi-natural picks this. A sown lawn is dominated by cultivated grass varieties, so it is not semi-natural.

A student who thinks semi-natural means untouched picks this. A bog with no human influence is a natural habitat, which is also acceptable for fieldwork, but the question asks which site is semi-natural: influenced by humans yet dominated by wild species.
questions.explain: A semi-natural habitat has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Annual cutting is human influence; the wild grasses and flowers that dominate make the meadow semi-natural.

questions.q: A biome distribution graph has mean annual temperature on one axis and mean annual precipitation on the other. Region X has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 150 mm of precipitation a year; region Y has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 3000 mm a year. What does the graph predict?
options: Hot desert is likely to develop in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because rainfall separates them at this temperature.
Tropical forest is likely in both regions, because it is the temperature of 26 °C that determines which biome forms.
Grassland is likely in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because grassland forms wherever it is too dry for trees.
No prediction is possible without knowing the latitude of each region, because latitude rather than climate sets the biome.
optionWhy: For any combination of temperature and rainfall pattern one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop. At 26 °C, precipitation below about 250 mm a year gives hot desert, while precipitation above about 2000 mm a year gives tropical forest.
A student who thinks temperature alone sets the biome picks this. The graph has two axes because both variables matter: 150 mm of rain a year cannot support forest at any temperature.
A student who extends grassland down to zero rainfall picks this. Grassland occupies an intermediate band of precipitation; below about 250 mm a year the graph shows desert.

A student who has memorized biomes as latitude bands picks this. Latitude matters only through its effect on climate; the graph predicts the biome from temperature and precipitation wherever on Earth the region is.
questions.explain: For any combination of temperature and rainfall pattern one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop. At 26 °C, precipitation below about 250 mm a year gives hot desert, while precipitation above about 2000 mm a year gives tropical forest.

questions.q: A biome has long, very cold winters, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil. Which biome is this?
options: Taiga, as in northern Canada
Hot desert, as in Arabia
Tundra, as in Arctic Canada
Grassland, as on the prairies
optionWhy: A student who treats the two cold northern biomes as interchangeable picks this. Taiga has long cold winters, but its short, mild summers give a growing season long enough, and its precipitation is sufficient, for coniferous forest to grow; a growing season of only a few weeks and permafrost are features of tundra.
A student who identifies a desert by low precipitation alone picks this. Precipitation below 250 mm is shared by hot desert and tundra; the very cold temperatures and frozen subsoil identify tundra.
Very cold temperatures, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permafrost are the climate conditions that characterize tundra, which supports low-growing plants but no trees.

A student who assigns any dry, treeless landscape to grassland picks this. Grassland has warmer growing seasons and, in temperate regions, more precipitation than 250 mm; the frozen subsoil and very short growing season are features of tundra.
questions.explain: Very cold temperatures, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permafrost are the climate conditions that characterize tundra, which supports low-growing plants but no trees.

questions.q: What is meant by the ecological niche of a species?
options: The role of the species in its ecosystem, including its biotic and abiotic interactions
The place where the species lives, described by its location and ecosystem type
The position of the species in a food chain, defined by the food it eats
The interactions of the species with other organisms, leaving out abiotic factors
optionWhy: This is the guide's definition. A niche is a role, described by the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence the species' growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food.
A student who equates niche with habitat picks this. The place in which a species lives is its habitat; the niche is what the species does in that place.
A student who thinks a niche is just a trophic level picks this. Obtaining food is one part of the niche, but predators, competitors and abiotic tolerances are also part of it.
A student who files abiotic conditions under 'habitat' picks this. The guidance includes abiotic interactions, such as tolerance of temperature or oxygen, in the niche.
questions.explain: This is the guide's definition. A niche is a role, described by the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence the species' growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food.

questions.q: Which statement about nutrition in animals is correct?
options: Animals that host photosynthetic algae inside their cells are autotrophic
Animals assimilate their food by absorbing it across the lining of the gut
Animals are heterotrophs that ingest, digest, absorb and assimilate food
Animals ingest food when digested molecules pass into their cells
optionWhy: A student who locates the mode of nutrition in the body rather than the organism picks this. The algae are autotrophs; the animal obtains carbon compounds from them and is heterotrophic.
A student who merges the two stages picks this. Passage across the gut wall is absorption; assimilation is the later use of the absorbed molecules in the animal's cells.
All animals are heterotrophic. Their holozoic nutrition consists of ingestion of food, internal digestion, absorption of the products and their assimilation into the animal's tissues.
A student who uses 'ingest' for uptake by cells picks this. Ingestion is taking food into the body at the start of holozoic nutrition, before digestion.
questions.explain: All animals are heterotrophic. Their holozoic nutrition consists of ingestion of food, internal digestion, absorption of the products and their assimilation into the animal's tissues.

questions.q: Which statement describes saprotrophic nutrition?
options: Secretion of enzymes onto dead organic matter, followed by absorption of the products of digestion
Ingestion of dead organic matter, followed by internal digestion and absorption of products
Any feeding on dead organic matter, whether by fungi and bacteria or by earthworms and woodlice
Synthesis of carbon compounds by fungi and bacteria that grow on dead organic matter
optionWhy: Saprotrophs such as many fungi and bacteria digest dead organic matter externally by secreting enzymes onto it and then absorb the soluble products. Organisms with this mode of nutrition can be referred to as decomposers.
A student who applies the animal model of digestion to fungi picks this. Saprotrophs do not ingest; they digest externally and absorb the products.

A student who uses 'decomposer' loosely picks this. Earthworms and woodlice ingest dead matter and digest it internally; saprotrophic nutrition is specifically external digestion by fungi and bacteria.
A student who thinks of fungi as plant-like picks this. Fungi and saprotrophic bacteria are heterotrophs; they obtain carbon compounds from the dead matter rather than synthesizing them.
questions.explain: Saprotrophs such as many fungi and bacteria digest dead organic matter externally by secreting enzymes onto it and then absorb the soluble products. Organisms with this mode of nutrition can be referred to as decomposers.

questions.q: Three species of archaea were studied. Species 1 obtains energy by oxidizing ammonia. Species 2 obtains energy by oxidizing carbon compounds absorbed from decaying matter. Species 3 obtains energy from light. What do these observations illustrate?
options: Archaea are a group of bacteria, so they show the same modes of nutrition as other bacteria
Archaea are metabolically diverse, using light, inorganic chemicals or carbon compounds
Archaea are chemosynthetic extremophiles, so only species 1 is a typical archaeon
Archaea are prokaryotes, so all three must be heterotrophs oxidizing carbon compounds
optionWhy: A student who still thinks of 'archaebacteria' picks this. Archaea are a separate domain of life from Bacteria; the observations illustrate diversity within that domain, not bacterial nutrition.

The three species use the three energy sources named in the guidance: oxidation of an inorganic chemical (species 1), oxidation of a carbon compound (species 2) and light (species 3). Archaea are metabolically very diverse.

A student who generalises from hot-spring examples picks this. All three are archaea; there is no single 'typical' archaeal metabolism, and many archaea live in ordinary soils and waters rather than extreme environments.
A student who thinks all prokaryotes are heterotrophic decomposers picks this. Only species 2 oxidizes carbon compounds; species 1 and 3 obtain energy from an inorganic chemical and from light.
questions.explain: The three species use the three energy sources named in the guidance: oxidation of an inorganic chemical (species 1), oxidation of a carbon compound (species 2) and light (species 3). Archaea are metabolically very diverse.

questions.q: An aphid feeds on a leaf without removing any tissue, whereas a caterpillar leaves ragged holes in the leaf. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The aphid has piercing mouthparts that reach the sap, whereas the caterpillar has chewing mouthparts that bite off leaf tissue
Both insects have chewing mouthparts, but the aphid is so small that the holes it bites are too tiny to be seen
The aphid pierces the leaf to inject a toxin that digests the tissue, whereas the caterpillar chews the tissue
Leaves are soft and undefended, so neither insect needs special mouthparts; the aphid is too small to remove visible tissue
optionWhy: Leaf-eating insects have either piercing or chewing mouthparts. An aphid's stylets penetrate the leaf to feed on sap without removing tissue; a caterpillar's mandibles cut and chew pieces of leaf.
A student who assumes all leaf-eating insects chew picks this. Aphids do not bite; they have piercing mouthparts and feed on sap, which is why no tissue is removed.
A student who links piercing insects with injecting picks this. The aphid's piercing mouthparts are a feeding adaptation for reaching sap, not for injecting a toxin.

A student who thinks plants offer no resistance picks this. Leaves are tough and often toxic, and the two insects differ because they have different mouthparts, piercing stylets in the aphid and chewing mandibles in the caterpillar, not because of size.
questions.explain: Leaf-eating insects have either piercing or chewing mouthparts. An aphid's stylets penetrate the leaf to feed on sap without removing tissue; a caterpillar's mandibles cut and chew pieces of leaf.

questions.q: On a rocky shore, adult barnacles of one species (Chthamalus) are found only high on the shore, while a second species (Balanus) occupies the middle and lower shore. When Balanus was removed from areas of the middle and lower shore, Chthamalus settled, survived and grew there. What do these results show?
options: Chthamalus is absent from the lower shore because the physical conditions there are beyond its tolerance limits
The fundamental niche of Chthamalus includes the lower shore, but competition restricts its realized niche
The realized niche of Chthamalus is the whole shore and its fundamental niche is the upper shore
Removing Balanus caused Chthamalus to adapt so that it could tolerate lower-shore conditions
optionWhy: A student who explains distribution by abiotic factors alone picks this. Chthamalus survived on the lower shore once Balanus was removed, so those conditions are within its tolerance.

The removal experiment shows Chthamalus can tolerate the lower shore, so it lies within its fundamental niche. In the presence of Balanus its realized niche, the extent actually occupied, is restricted to the upper shore by competition.
A student who inverts the two terms picks this. The fundamental niche is the potential (whole shore); the realized niche is the actual extent in competition (upper shore only).
A student who thinks tolerance changes in response to circumstances picks this. The tolerance limits of Chthamalus were unchanged; it occupied more of a fundamental niche it already had.
questions.explain: The removal experiment shows Chthamalus can tolerate the lower shore, so it lies within its fundamental niche. In the presence of Balanus its realized niche, the extent actually occupied, is restricted to the upper shore by competition.
